mainTopic: Why a בתולה marries on Wednesday, and when a groom whose wedding is delayed must start feeding his bride
overview: The opening משנה of כתובות says a בתולה marries on Wednesday and an אלמנה on Thursday, because courts sit on Monday and Thursday and a husband with a טענת בתולים can go to court the next morning. רב יוסף first reports that שמואל tied this rule to a later משנה about when a groom must start feeding his bride, and then objects. Why explain a rule whose reason is stated openly through a rule whose reason is not stated? So the גמרא gives a corrected version of שמואל: Wednesday is for the court day. The גמרא then asks why Sunday would not work just as well. It answers that the חכמים wanted the groom to spend Sunday through Tuesday preparing the wedding feast (שקדו). From this the גמרא learns that a groom whose wedding date falls on Sunday does not owe food until Wednesday. One version extends this to illness and נדה. Another version turns these cases into a ladder of questions: his illness, her illness, and her becoming a נדה. The amud ends by setting aside the case of a period at her expected time, and the question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The משנה: Virgins Marry on Wednesday, Widows on Thursday
steps.stepSummary: The משנה sets the wedding days and explains why a בתולה marries on Wednesday.
steps.simpleTranslation: A virgin is married on Wednesday and a widow on Thursday. This is because courts sit in the towns twice a week, on Monday and Thursday. So if the husband has a claim about her virginity, he can go to court early the next morning.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the set days for weddings and explains the reason for the בתולה's day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wedding on Wednesday means the marriage is completed Wednesday night. If the husband finds a problem with her virginity, Thursday is a court day, so he can bring his claim right away while he is still upset. The משנה states this reason openly.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman who was never married (a virgin)
A widow
Is married (the actual wedding, נישואין)
Courts
A husband's claim that his bride was not a virgin
Goes early in the morning

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה itself tells us the reason for Wednesday: so a טענת בתולים can go to court on Thursday morning.

phrases.english: A virgin is married on the fourth day (Wednesday)
and a widow on the fifth day (Thursday).
For twice a week
phrases.notes: Here שַׁבָּת means 'week,' not the day of שבת.

phrases.english: courts sit in the towns:
on the second day (Monday) and on the fifth day (Thursday),
so that if he had a claim about her virginity,
he would go early to court.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A בתולה marries on Wednesday and an אלמנה on Thursday, because courts sit Monday and Thursday and a טענת בתולים can then be brought right away.

steps.title: שמואל Asks Why a Virgin Marries on Wednesday
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with שמואל, who asks why the משנה chose Wednesday.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said in the name of רב יהודה, who said in the name of שמואל: For what reason did they say a virgin is married on Wednesday?
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל asks why the rule of Wednesday exists. This question sets up his own answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is surprising, because the משנה already gave a reason (the court days). שמואל is about to give another reason, and that is exactly what רב יוסף will object to later.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
For what reason?

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not asked because the משנה gave no reason. The משנה did give one. שמואל is adding a different reason, and that is what causes the problem later.

phrases.english: Gemara

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said that Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
For what reason did they say
that a virgin is married on Wednesday?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the משנה's rule in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the משנה set Wednesday as the wedding day for a בתולה.

steps.title: שמואל Links Wednesday to When Support Begins
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains the Wednesday rule using a later משנה about a groom who delays the wedding.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because we learned: if the set time arrived and they did not marry, the brides eat from his food and eat תרומה. You might think that if the time arrived on Sunday, he must start feeding her from Sunday. That is why we learned: a virgin is married on Wednesday.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers his own question by pointing to a later משנה about a groom who must feed his bride once the wedding date passes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The later משנה says that once the wedding date arrives and the wedding does not happen, the groom must support her. שמואל says our משנה teaches that the 'time' only counts as arriving on Wednesday, since that is the wedding day. So if the date fell on Sunday, he does not owe support until Wednesday.

keyTerms.meaning: Because we learned (in a משנה)
The set time arrived
The כהן's portion of produce, which only a כהן's household may eat
One might think
Food support

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole objection that follows: שמואל explains a clear rule by tying it to a different rule that is less clear.

phrases.english: Because we learned:
If the time arrived and they were not married,
they eat from his food, and they eat terumah.
phrases.notes: Eating תרומה applies if the groom is a כהן.

phrases.english: One might think: if the time arrived on Sunday,
he would have to provide her food?
Therefore we learned:
A virgin is married on Wednesday.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The Wednesday rule teaches that the groom's duty to support her does not start before Wednesday, even if the set date was earlier in the week.

steps.title: רב יוסף Objects in Amazement
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף is shocked that שמואל explains a taught rule with something that is 'not taught.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: Master of אברהם! He hangs what is taught on what is not taught?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף strongly objects to the explanation he himself just reported in the name of שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף's complaint: our משנה is clear, so why explain it through another source? His exact wording, 'not taught,' seems odd, and the גמרא will question it next.

keyTerms.meaning: Master of אברהם! (a cry of amazement)
Hangs, makes dependent

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
Master of Avraham!
phrases.notes: He is calling out to ה׳ in surprise, like saying 'Oh my God!'

phrases.english: He hangs what is taught on what is not taught?!

steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's explanation of the Wednesday rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It makes no sense to explain a rule that is clearly taught by pointing to something that is not clearly taught.

steps.title: But Both Sources Are Taught!
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions רב יוסף's wording: both sources are משניות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which one is taught and which one is not taught? This one is taught and that one is taught!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what רב יוסף meant, since both rules come from משניות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה and the later משנה are both written in the משנה. So 'not taught' cannot be meant literally. This sets up the next step, which explains what רב יוסף really meant.

keyTerms.meaning: Which one?
This one

phrases.english: Which is taught and which is not taught?
This is taught and that is taught!
phrases.notes: Both are משניות: ours here and the one on דף נ״ז.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of רב יוסף's objection in step 4.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both rules appear in a משנה, so neither can be called 'not taught.'

steps.title: What רב יוסף Really Meant
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף's point: שמואל made a rule with a stated reason depend on a rule with no stated reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he hangs a taught rule that explains its reason on a taught rule that does not explain its reason.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רב יוסף's objection: 'taught' and 'not taught' really mean 'reason stated' and 'reason not stated.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה openly gives its reason (the court days). The later משנה about support gives no reason for its timing. So bringing in the later משנה adds nothing to understanding ours. That is רב יוסף's real complaint against שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (introduces the corrected meaning)
Explains its reason

steps.whatToRemember: רב יוסף's objection is that our משנה already gives its own reason, so tying it to a משנה with no stated reason does not help explain it.

phrases.english: Rather:
he hangs a taught rule that explains its reason
on a taught rule that does not explain its reason.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5 by reinterpreting רב יוסף's words.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Not taught' meant a rule that is not in the משנה at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Not taught' means a rule whose reason is not stated. Our משנה states its reason; the later one does not.

steps.title: The corrected version of שמואל's teaching
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the earlier version of שמואל's statement and gives a new one. Wednesday was chosen so that a groom with a virginity claim can go to court the next morning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if שמואל said something, this is what he said. רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: Why did the חכמים say a בתולה marries on Wednesday? So that if the groom has a טענת בתולים, he can go early the next morning to בית דין.
steps.whatsHappening: Since רב יוסף's attack showed the first version of שמואל was a problem, the גמרא starts over with a different version of what שמואל actually said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the old version, שמואל tied the Wednesday rule to the later משנה about delayed weddings. That is what רב יוסף objected to. In the new version, שמואל simply gives the reason the משנה itself states: בית דין meets on Thursday, so the groom can bring his claim right away.

keyTerms.meaning: If it was said, this is how it was said. This introduces a corrected version of a teaching.
A groom's claim that his bride was not a virgin
Goes early to the court

phrases.english: Rather, if it was stated, this is how it was stated.
phrases.notes: The גמרא is setting aside the earlier version of שמואל and giving the version it accepts.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
For what reason did they say
that a virgin is married on Wednesday?
So that if he had a claim about her virginity,
he would go early to court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the version of שמואל that רב יוסף attacked in steps 4-6 with a new version.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wednesday was chosen so that a groom with a טענת בתולים can go to בית דין early Thursday morning.

steps.title: Why not marry on Sunday instead?
steps.stepSummary: If the goal is to be near a court day, Sunday would work just as well, since court also meets on Monday.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let her marry on Sunday! Then too, if he had a טענת בתולים, he could go early the next morning to בית דין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason it just gave: that reason does not explain why Wednesday was picked over Sunday.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית דין meets on both Monday and Thursday. So a Sunday wedding would also let the groom go to court the very next morning. The reason given so far fits two days, yet the משנה picked only one.

keyTerms.meaning: Sunday, the first day of the week
So let her marry. This is a challenging suggestion.

phrases.english: But let her marry on Sunday,
since if he had a claim about her virginity
he would go early to court!
phrases.notes: Court also sits on Monday, so Sunday seems to work just as well.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in step 7 as not being enough.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason that Wednesday was chosen because of the court day
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Sunday is also the day before a court day, so the reason does not explain why Wednesday was chosen.

steps.title: The חכמים wanted a proper wedding feast
steps.stepSummary: Wednesday was chosen so the groom would have Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday to prepare the feast. This was for the bride's honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים cared deeply about the well-being of Jewish women. They wanted the groom to work on the feast for three days, Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday, and then marry her on Wednesday.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a second reason works together with the court-day reason. Only Wednesday satisfies both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court-day reason alone fits both Sunday and Wednesday. The חכמים added a second concern: the groom should spend three full days, Sunday through Tuesday, preparing the feast. Only Wednesday satisfies both reasons.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים were careful and diligent
The well-being of Jewish women
Works hard preparing the feast
He marries her and brings her into his home

steps.whyThisMatters: This reason, שקדו, is the basis for the next steps about the groom's duty to feed his bride.

phrases.english: The Sages were diligent
about the well-being of Jewish women,
so that he would work on the feast for three days,
Sunday and Monday
and Tuesday,
and on Wednesday he marries her.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁקְדוּ חֲכָמִים עַל תַּקָּנַת בְּנוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the Sunday challenge from step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds a second reason that rules out Sunday
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The court-day reason alone should allow Sunday.
steps.terutzMaskana: Wednesday is required both for the court day and for three days of feast preparation.

steps.title: A Sunday deadline does not obligate food yet
steps.stepSummary: Because of שקדו, if the groom's deadline falls on Sunday, he does not have to feed the bride until Wednesday.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that we learned the reason is שקדו, look at the משנה that says: 'If the time came and they did not marry, the brides eat from his food and eat תרומה.' If the time came on Sunday, he cannot marry her yet, so he does not have to provide her food.
steps.whatsHappening: Using the שקדו reason, the גמרא draws a practical rule about the later משנה on delayed weddings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, once the deadline passes, the groom must feed the bride. But a Sunday deadline is not his fault, because the חכמים' rule keeps him from marrying her until Wednesday. So he is exempt until then.

keyTerms.meaning: The set time for the wedding arrived
They eat from his food. He must support them.
The portion of produce given to a כהן, which his household may eat
Provides her with food

phrases.english: And now that we learned 'they were diligent,'
that which we learned:
'If the time arrived and they did not marry,
phrases.notes: This is the later משנה about a groom who delays the wedding, the same one שמואל used in step 3.

phrases.english: they eat from his food and eat teruma,'
if the time arrived on Sunday,
since he is unable to marry her,
he does not provide her food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the שקדו reason from step 9 to the later משנה about the bride's food.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A groom whose deadline falls on Sunday is exempt from feeding the bride until Wednesday, because the חכמים' rule prevents the wedding.

steps.title: Extending the exemption to illness and נדה
steps.stepSummary: By the same logic, if the wedding is delayed by his illness, her illness, or her becoming a נדה, he does not have to feed her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore: if he got sick, or she got sick, or she became a נדה, he does not provide her food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stretches the Sunday rule to other delays that are not the groom's choice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that the groom only owes food when the delay is his fault. Illness or נדה stops the wedding the same way the Sunday rule does, so he is exempt here too.

keyTerms.meaning: Therefore
She began to menstruate and became a נדה

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the cases. Sunday is a delay caused by the חכמים' own rule. Illness and נדה are delays caused by life. This step treats them the same, but the next step questions that for the groom's illness.

phrases.aramaic: לְפִיכָךְ: חָלָה הוּא אוֹ שֶׁחָלְתָה הִיא
phrases.english: Therefore: if he fell ill or she fell ill
or she began to menstruate,
he does not provide her food.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְפִיכָךְ חָלָה הוּא אוֹ שֶׁחָלְתָה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the exemption from step 10 to other unavoidable delays.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Any delay forced on the groom, such as illness or נדה, exempts him from feeding the bride.

steps.title: An open question about the groom's illness
steps.stepSummary: Another version does not state the illness rule. It asks whether the groom's illness is like the Sunday case or different from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some raise it as a question: if he got sick, what is the law? In the Sunday case, the reason is that he was forced, and here too he is forced. Or perhaps there, he was forced by a rule the חכמים made, and here not.
steps.whatsHappening: Instead of a clear rule, this version leaves the case of the groom's illness as an undecided question with two sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: the Sunday exemption is about being forced (אנוס), and a sick groom is also forced. Side two: the Sunday exemption exists because the חכמים themselves caused the delay with their own rule. Ordinary illness is not their doing, so maybe he still has to feed her.

keyTerms.meaning: Some raise it as an open question
He is forced by circumstances beyond his control
Or perhaps. This introduces the other side of a question.
A rule that the חכמים made

steps.whatToRemember: The Sunday exemption could rest on one of two ideas. Either any forced delay frees the groom from feeding her, or only a delay caused by the חכמים' own rule does. The groom's illness is the test case between them.

phrases.english: And there are those who raise it as a question:
If he fell ill, what is the law?
There, what is the reason? Because he was forced,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the case where the deadline fell on Sunday.

phrases.english: and here too, he is forced.
Or perhaps:
there he was forced by an ordinance
that the Sages instituted for him,
here, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of step 11, where the groom's illness is a question instead of a stated rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the groom's illness exempt him from feeding the bride, like the Sunday deadline does?

steps.title: What if the bride is the one who gets sick?
steps.stepSummary: Assuming the groom must feed her when he is sick, the גמרא asks about the case where she is sick. Can he say 'I'm ready,' or can she say 'his field was flooded'?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say that when he got sick he gives her food, what about when she got sick? Can he say to her, 'Here I am, ready'? Or maybe she can say to him, 'His field has been flooded'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא assumes one possible answer to the question from step 12: the groom pays when he is sick. Then it asks the next question up the ladder: what if the bride is the sick one?
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the groom is sick, the delay comes from his side, so it makes sense for him to pay. When she is sick, he has a strong argument: 'I am standing ready, the delay is from you.' She has a counter-argument: this bad luck counts as his loss, like a flood that hits a man's own field.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say. Assumes one answer to the earlier question, then builds a new question on top of it.
What is the law? This is the standard way to open a question.
Food and support that the groom provides for the bride.
Here I am, standing ready. The groom's claim that the delay is not his fault.
His field has been flooded. The bad luck counts as the owner's loss.

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא has not decided yet that the groom pays when he is sick. 'ואם תמצי לומר' only means 'IF you answer that way.' The earlier question is still open.

phrases.english: And if you will say
phrases.notes: This builds on the question from the last step: is the groom's illness like the Sunday case?

phrases.english: that if he got sick, he provides her food,
if she got sick, what is the law?
Can he say to her:
"Here I am, standing ready",
or perhaps she can say to him:
"His field has been flooded".
phrases.notes: She means her illness is like a disaster that hit his own field, so the loss is his.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּמְצֵי לוֹמַר חָלָה הוּא מַעֲלֶה לָהּ מְזוֹנוֹת חָלְתָה הִיא מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Assumes one answer to step 12's question and moves to a harder case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the groom must feed the bride when the delay comes from HER illness: is it 'I am ready' or 'his field was flooded'?

steps.title: What if the bride becomes a נדה?
steps.stepSummary: Assuming she wins with 'his field was flooded' when she is sick, the גמרא asks about the case where she becomes a נדה and the wedding is delayed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say that she can tell him 'his field was flooded,' what if she became a נדה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא climbs one more step on the ladder. It assumes she wins the illness case and asks about a delay caused by her becoming a נדה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Illness is a sudden, unexpected accident, so it fits the 'flooded field' idea. Becoming a נדה is a different kind of delay, so the גמרא asks whether the same reasoning still holds.

keyTerms.meaning: She became a נדה. Her period began, so the wedding is delayed.

phrases.english: And if you will say
that she can say to him, "His field has been flooded,"
if she became a נדה, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּמְצֵי לוֹמַר אָמְרָה לֵיהּ נִסְתַּחֲפָה שָׂדֵהוּ פֵּירְסָה נִדָּה מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Assumes the bride wins in step 13 and asks about the next, harder case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a delay caused by her becoming a נדה is treated like her illness, so that the groom must still feed her.

steps.title: Narrowing the question: her expected time needs no question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to limit the נדה question. If she became a נדה at the time of her expected period, there is no question to ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: At the time of her expected period, you do not need to ask.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is narrowing the question from step 14. It says one case is not in doubt: when her period came at its expected time. This sets up the next move, which gives the reason and the case that IS in doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not every case of becoming a נדה is the same. A period that comes at its expected time is different from one that comes by surprise, and the גמרא takes the expected case off the table. The גמרא continues this on the next amud, so do not fill in the answer yet.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman's expected, regular time for her period.
You do not need to ask. This case is clear, so the question does not apply to it.

phrases.english: At the time of her expected period,
you need not ask,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refines the question of step 14 by setting aside the case of a period at its expected time, which is not in doubt.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Partial: the case of a period at its expected time is not in doubt. The reason and the remaining doubtful case come next.
